newsitem.title: ITALY: "Villa of Hope" reeks of despair for Albanians.
newsitem.headline: "Villa of Hope" reeks of despair for Albanians.

text.p: It is called the Villa of Hope but few of its bedraggled residents appreciate the irony.

One of the "hospitality centres" for Albanian refugees set up by an Italian charity, the Villa Della Speranza, a former orphanage, houses some of the youngest among the 8,000 who have fled to Italy in a flotilla of rusty boats.

About 50 of the ragged children it holds came over without their parents, left behind in Albania's anarchy. It also houses one young mother who fled without her six-month-old daughter, reasoning the child was too tiny to risk the crossing.
The children pass their time playing soccer in a garden of the villa, which overlooks the Adriatic Sea.
"There was war in Vlore. We came here to escape, for political asylum. Everybody in Vlore has weapons and no-one knows who is in control," said Beneto Prapai, at 14 the youngest of the refugees.

Beneto, like his friends, looks no angel. All exude street-savvy and walk with swaggers in the palm-lined garden of the run-down villa, which is used as a summer retreat by the local Roman Catholic Church.
Beneto shows no emotion over the separation from his family.
"Now I want my parents to come over. I haven't been able to contact them because I don't have money to make the calls," he said, speaking through another teenager who acted as interpreter.
Asked what he would do if he had to choose between staying in Italy without his parents or returning to Albania to be with them, Beneto said: "I want my parents to come here".
His friend Teodor Sota, 15, said: "I have hope for the future only if I stay in Italy."
Father Giuseppe Satriano, a local Roman Catholic priest, helps co-ordinate volunteers at the villa.
"These kids are a tragedy within a tragedy," he said.
Local women spent Tuesday morning distributing used clothes and shoes donated by the people of Ostuni, a small hill town above the coast about 25 km (15 miles) north of the seaport of Brindisi.
Other volunteers disinfected floors where the boys sleep 25 to a room.
The other residents of the Villa of Hope are families.

Luan Shpati, 29 and his wife Brikena, 28, tell what is perhaps the most poignant tale among them. They came over from the port of Durres with their son Rexhers, aged three, but decided to leave their six-month-old daughter, Sara, behind.
"She was too small. We didn't think she would make it," said Luan. The mother said she "left her with a friend" in the hope that the Italians could bring the child over to them later.

The Shpatis said they paid some two million lire ($1,200) to racketeers in Durres to make the 13-hour trip on a jam-packed fishing boat to a southern Italian port, an account repeated by many of the recent refugees.
"We sold the car and the house to get here," the woman said through an interpreter. "We have nothing left".
